edges.effect_quant: In 584 older women from the Nurses' Health Study, each standard-deviation increase in tibia lead was associated with an excess annual decline in overall cognitive score of about 0.024 standard units. In 1,001 adults aged 50 to 70 years from the Baltimore Memory Study, higher cumulative tibia lead was associated with worse performance in several late-life cognitive domains, especially under higher neighborhood psychosocial stress. A meta-analysis of 3,849 adults also found that every 10 micrograms per deciliter increase in blood lead translated into a cognitive decline of about Hedges g 0.09.
edges.population: older adults and late-middle-aged adults with cumulative environmental lead exposure
edges.mechanism: Lead accumulates in bone and can continue to redistribute over time, creating a long-tail exposure even after external sources decline. In older adults, that cumulative burden may amplify neuroinflammation, vascular injury, and synaptic dysfunction that show up as faster cognitive aging rather than dramatic poisoning.
edges.summary: The clearest signal is cumulative rather than current lead. Older adults with more lifetime lead burden appear to age cognitively a bit faster, especially on memory, fluency, and executive-type tasks.
edges.caveats: The effect size is modest, and some cohorts show domain-specific rather than global cognitive associations. This edge should be read as a contributor to cognitive aging risk, not as a single dominant cause of dementia on its own.
